blocks.text: When a body is deformed by a force, work is done against the elastic restoring force. It is stored in the body as its potential energy and equals the gain in potential energy of the molecules of the body due to their displacement from their mean positions.
Derivation of the expression for the energy stored in a stretched material

Consider a material in the form of a spring (Fig. 5.6) stretched by a force F through an extension x. As the extension is directly proportional to the stretching force within the elastic limit, the force increases uniformly from zero to F (Fig. 5.7); thus the average force that stretches the spring through delta x is (1/2) F. Hence the work done by the stretching force is work done = average force x distance in the direction of the force: W = (1/2) F x delta x ... (5.7). From Hooke's law F = k (delta x), therefore W = ((1/2) k delta x)(delta x) = (1/2) k (delta x)^2, or W = area of OPQ. The work done by the stretching force is stored in the spring as its strain energy and equals the potential energy stored in its molecules: strain energy stored in the body = E = (1/2) F delta x = (1/2) k (delta x)^2. The amount of work done in stretching a material equals the average force applied multiplied by the distance moved, so the area under a force-extension graph represents the work done to stretch the material, which also equals the elastic PE stored in it (For Your Information).

blocks.alt: Two springs hang from a support: the left one at its original length, the right one stretched by a weight that pulls down with force F. A green double arrow marks the extension x. A box gives F = k x and the stored energy (1/2) F x = (1/2) k x^2.
blocks.caption: A spring stretched by a force F through x (original diagram after Figure 5.6).

blocks.alt: A graph of force against extension: a straight line from O rises to P at force F and extension x. The triangle OPQ under it is shaded and labelled area = (1/2) F x, the energy stored in the spring.
blocks.caption: Force against extension: the area OPQ is the stored energy (original diagram after Figure 5.7).

blocks.text: Let A be the cross-sectional area of the material of length L and delta L the extension; then the volume of the material is A L. The strain energy per unit volume of the material is U = (1/2) (F x delta L) / (A x L), or U = (1/2) x (F/A) x (delta L / L) ... (5.8), or U = (1/2) x stress x strain ... (5.9). From the equation of Young's modulus (Eq. 5.6), F/A = Y x delta L / L; putting this in Eq. 5.8, the strain energy per unit volume is U = (1/2) Y x (delta L / L) x (delta L / L) = (1/2) Y (delta L / L)^2 ... (5.10). This equation is used to calculate the strain energy stored in the material when it is stressed.

blocks.caption: Strain energy
rows: W = (1/2) F delta x = (1/2) k (delta x)^2 = area OPQ under the F against delta x line (5.7)

blocks.prompt: A spring of constant 200 N m^-1 is stretched by 0.5 m; find the elastic PE stored (numerical 5.2). Why is the stored energy half the product F delta x and not the full product?
blocks.explanation: E = (1/2) k x^2 = (1/2) x 200 x 0.25 = 25 J. The force is not constant: it grows from zero to F as the spring stretches, so only the average force F/2 acts over the whole extension, which the triangle under the force-extension line shows.

items: Work against the restoring force is stored as strain (elastic potential) energy. Spring: average force F/2, W = (1/2) F delta x = (1/2) k (delta x)^2 = area OPQ. Per unit volume U = (1/2) stress x strain = (1/2) Y (delta L/L)^2.
